extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent applicants/patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the 'markedly different characteristics' comparison when evaluating whether a claimed nature-based product is a 'product of nature' exception under patent eligibility (Alice/Mayo framework Step 2A). Applies to claims reciting nature-based products in various claim types (product, product-by-process, process, combinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to apply markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations in a claim; do not overextend the analysis to claim elements that are not nature-based. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the analysis; if it is not naturally occurring (e.g., due to human intervention), then perform the analysis to determine whether it is a product of nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis compares the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. Example distinctions: a claim to 'a Lactobacillus bacterium' should be analyzed as a nature-based product; a claim to a kit containing Lactobacillus plus non-nature elements should have only the nature-based limitation analyzed here (the other elements are evaluated later in Prong Two or Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims: analyze the entire claimed nature-based product
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim is to a nature-based product by itself, apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to the entire claimed product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a nature-based combination produced by combining components (e.g., 'a probiotic composition comprising a mixture of Lactobacillus and milk'), analyze the resultant combination rather than each component separately. If the claim is solely a nature-based product and a marked difference is shown, no further Step 2A/2B analysis is necessary for the product-of-nature question (the claim would be NO at Step 2A Pathway B unless another exception is present). Case example: Chakrabarty applied analysis to the entire genetically modified bacterium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims combining nature-based and non-nature elements: limit analysis to the nature-based limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim includes a nature-based product in combination with non-nature elements, perform the markedly different characteristics analysis only on the nature-based product limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-nature elements (e.g., containers, instructions) are not subject to this analysis but will be considered later in Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed) if the nature-based product is found to lack marked differences. Example: in a 'yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions', analyze the Lactobacillus for marked differences; the container and instructions are evaluated separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: focus on whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: For product-by-process claims, the markedly different characteristics analysis turns on whether the nature-based product recited in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2113 for additional product-by-process claim guidance. The analysis centers on the product itself (what it is) rather than the recited process steps when determining marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: generally not subject unless effectively claiming a product
rubrics_metrics.description: Process claims are generally not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process, because process analysis should focus on the active steps rather than ingredients. However, if a process claim is drafted so that it is, in substance, no different from a product claim (i.e., focuses on the product), then it is subject to the markedly different analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a claim for a method of cryopreserving hepatocytes was evaluated as a process (not subject to marked difference analysis for the hepatocytes). Conversely, a claim such as 'a method of providing an apple' would be treated as focused on the apple (a product) and thus subject to the product-oriented marked-difference analysis. Ariosa/Sequenom-related holdings on detecting naturally occurring materials illustrate when process claims can be product-directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is to select the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to which the claimed nature-based product will be compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, the natural thing from which it was derived is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A derived from acid A — acid A is the counterpart). Do not confuse the counterpart with adjacent naturally occurring material (e.g., compare an isolated gene to the gene, not the entire chromosome). When multiple possible counterparts exist, select the closest naturally occurring counterpart based on the examiner’s expertise (e.g., choose the most closely related breed in a cloned-animal example). For claimed mixtures with no natural counterpart, compare to the individual naturally occurring components. Best practice: if rejecting as ineligible, identify the selected counterpart in the Office action to assist the applicant and clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying appropriate characteristics to compare
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify characteristics possessed by the claimed product (as defined by the claim language and its broadest reasonable interpretation) to use in the comparison to the natural counterpart; characteristics may be structural, functional, or other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product — unclaimed characteristics cannot be relied on. Characteristics can be explicit in the claim (e.g., chemical name indicating structure) or inferred from the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., 'isolated gene B' implies nucleotide sequence and encoded protein). Courts consider structure, function, and other properties. Non-limiting example categories: biological/pharmacological functions (e.g., protein-encoding information; binding ability), chemical/physical properties (alkalinity, ductility), phenotype (shape, size, color, behavior), and structure/form (plasmids presence, chemical/crystalline form, nucleotide sequence, genotype).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating whether characteristics are 'markedly different'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed product’s characteristics to the naturally occurring counterpart’s characteristics to determine whether they are 'markedly different' — a characteristic must be changed compared to nature and not merely inherent, incidental, or innate to the natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a marked difference, the claimed product must possess at least one characteristic that is different from the counterpart, and that change must have come about or been produced by the applicant’s efforts or influences. Incidental changes or characteristics innate to the natural counterpart do not qualify (e.g., isolation-induced end differences were insufficient in Myriad). If no changed characteristic exists, the claimed product is a product of nature exception and requires further analysis (Prong Two). If a changed characteristic exists and is caused by applicant, the product will generally be considered not a product of nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome rule based on analysis result
rubrics_metrics.description: If the nature-based product limitation exhibits markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart, the limitation is not a product of nature exception and the claim is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B) unless another exception is recited; if the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics, it is a product of nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (and possibly Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, showing a marked difference ends the product-of-nature inquiry (Step 2B not necessary). For claims including additional limitations, examiners must consider whether other exceptions are recited that would require additional eligibility analysis. Examples: Chakrabarty and Myriad illustrate opposite outcomes: Chakrabarty’s genetically modified bacterium had markedly different structural and functional characteristics and was eligible; Myriad’s isolated genes lacked marked differences (isolation alone insufficient) and were product-of-nature exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Court decisions provide examples of products that either possess or lack markedly different characteristics to guide application of the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of marked differences: Chakrabarty’s bacterium (additional plasmids and ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons); Myriad’s cDNA (structurally different exon-only nucleotide sequence). Examples lacking marked differences: Myriad’s isolated genomic BRCA genes (isolation alone is incidental change), Ambry primers (single-stranded primers had the same nucleotide sequence and innate binding function), Roslin clones (cloned animals were genetic copies lacking claimed marked differences; unclaimed phenotypic variances cannot establish marked difference), In re Marden (ductility an inherent characteristic). These examples illustrate anti-patterns (changes that are incidental, innate, or unclaimed will not establish marked difference) and support application of the evaluation guidance above.
